messages.content: my brother wants to play with a ball in our room, and i want to build a toy house on the floor. there is not much space. help us talk about it without choosing for us.
you could start with what each of you needs: i need space on the floor for the house. what space do you need for your game? then you can look at whether both things can happen together.
he says the ball might break my house. i do not want that.
then doing both in the same small space may not work well. you could choose different rooms if there is another place, or use this room one after the other.
we only have this room now. i need the floor for a while, but he wants to start too.

you can ask whether he would like to help build first or choose another quiet game while you use the floor. he can also ask how long you need. the answer should be something both of you understand, rather than one person having to read the other mind.
write a short conversation where he chooses to help for now.

i need the floor for the house. the ball could break it. would you like to help me build first? yes, but can we make a place for my game later? we can talk about that when the house is done. then i will help with the roof.
did that last conversation choose a specific hour for his game?
no. it says they will talk after the house is done. if he needs a clear time, they should choose that before starting.
make that answer simple.
no. they did not choose an hour. they should talk about the time before they start if that is important to him.
tell me a story about a child reading a hard line while a mother gives help without taking over the whole page.

a child opens a book and starts a line slowly. her mother knows the next word but waits. the child tries it, stops, and asks for help. her mother says the word, then asks whether she would like to try the line again. the child reads it from the start and gets through the hard part. she wants to read the next line herself. her mother is still near and listens, giving help only when the child asks or seems lost. by the end of the page, the child has done most of the reading and knows she can ask when she needs someone.
use is still near in the sentence about her mother.
her mother is still near and listens, giving help when the child asks or seems lost.
why did the mother wait instead of saying every word first?
she wanted to give the child room to try. knowing an answer does not always mean saying it before the other person has time to think.
did she say she would not help?
no. she gave the word when the child asked. waiting for a try and never helping are different things.
ask my last question simply.
did she say she would not help?
what could the mother ask before the next page?
would you like to read this part yourself, or shall we read it together?
i have a drawing of a tree from last year and a photo of the same tree today. can i use them to say how much it grew?
you can look for changes, but the drawing may not give the same kind of detail as a photo. the tree could look larger because of how the person drew it or where someone stood for the photo.
answer simply.
the drawing may make the tree look smaller or larger than it really was. the two pictures alone may not tell you how much it grew.
what can i say without choosing a size i do not know?
you could write: this is my drawing of the tree from last year, and this is a photo from today. it looks different to me, but i do not know how much it grew.
what if i know the tree was below a window last year and is above it now?
that gives a more specific detail if the window and your way of looking are the same. you can say the top was below the window before and is above it now, rather than making up a number.
write that in two short sentences.
last year, the top of the tree was below the window. today, it is above the window.
does that say every part of the tree grew in the same way?
no. it only gives the place of the top near the window. it does not give every detail about the whole tree.
answer simply.
no. we know about the top and window, rather than every part of the tree.
i need to return a book and a cup to my cousin. the book can wait, but they need the cup tomorrow. help me write a clear message.
i can return your cup tomorrow. would it be okay to bring the book another day?
why not ask whether both things can wait?
your cousin already needs the cup tomorrow. asking about both as if the need were the same could make the message less clear. say when the cup can come, then ask about the book.
say it simply.
say when you can bring the cup, then ask about the book. the two things have different needs in this plan.
now my cousin says tomorrow is okay for the cup, but they would like the book back today.
then you have a new detail about the book. do you have a way to return it today, or do you need to say you cannot?
i cannot return it today. i can bring both tomorrow.
you could write: i am sorry, but i cannot return the book today. i can bring both the book and cup tomorrow. would that work for you?
can i say the whole plan is chosen after sending the message?
not until your cousin answers. you have given what you can do, but the other person may still need to talk about it.
answer simply.
no. your message gives a possible plan. your cousin still needs to answer.
i heard a new song once and now i feel i know it. is that the same as knowing every word?
not always. you might know the sound or remember one part without knowing all the words. try saying what you remember and see which parts are clear.
i remember the first line and the end. the middle is not clear.
then you know some parts, while another part still needs listening. you can enjoy what you know without saying you know the whole song.
say it simply.
you know the first line and the end, but not the whole song. you can listen again for the middle.
write a short request to someone who knows it.
could you sing the middle part slowly? i remember the first line and the end, but not the words between them.
what if they cannot remember it either?
then neither of you knows that part right now. you can leave it open. if you make up new words, keep them as a new part, not as words you know were in the old song.
make that answer simple.
you can leave the middle open. if you make up new words, keep them as a new part, not as words you know were in the old song.
can we still sing the parts we know?
yes. you can sing those parts and say that the middle is not remembered yet.
i took two pictures of one chair, first in the kitchen and then in the bedroom. my child thinks there are two chairs because the places are different.
you can explain that a picture gives one moment. the same chair can be moved and be in another picture in a different room. two pictures do not always mean two different objects.
say it simply.
one chair can be in the kitchen first and the bedroom later. two pictures can show the same chair in different places.
write a small story where we show the child the move.

a child looks at a picture of a chair in the kitchen and another in the bedroom. her father takes the chair from the bedroom back to the kitchen while she watches. she sees that it is one chair going between the rooms. he asks how many real chairs are in this example, and she says one. then he asks how many pictures there are, and she says two.
now i add another real chair in the kitchen. what changes?
then you have two real chairs: the first chair and the new one. the new chair makes two, while moving the first chair did not change the number.
use makes two in a short answer.
the new chair makes two real chairs. moving the first chair only changed where it was.
write one sentence to help the child remember the idea.
count the real chairs, not each picture as a new chair.
my friend said i understand what you need, but i cannot do it today. did they say my request was not clear?
no. they said they understood the request. not doing it today is different from not understanding it.
answer simply.
no. they know what you asked, but cannot do it today.
what can i ask next if another day would work?
you could ask: is there another day when you would have time, or should i ask someone else?
what if i need it today for sure?
then tell them that and look for another way to get help. you do not need to explain the same request again if the problem is time rather than meaning.
write a kind reply if i choose to ask someone else.
thank you for telling me. i need it today, so i will ask someone else. i understand that you do not have time.
say my last request simply.
write a kind reply saying i will ask someone else because i need it today.
does asking someone else mean i am not happy with my friend?
not by itself. it can simply mean you need help at a time when your friend cannot give it.
ask my last question simply.
does asking someone else mean i am not happy with my friend?
i know my friend took a train, but i do not know where they got off. can i say they went to town?
not unless you know that detail too. taking a train does not choose the end place from the information you gave.
what can i ask them?
where did you get off the train?
they say at a station near a village. can i now say they live in the village?
no. getting off near a village does not tell you where they live. they could be visiting, working, or meeting someone there.
write a short conversation that asks about the stop and then asks why the person went there.
where did you get off? near the village. do you live there? no, i came to meet my aunt. so you are visiting today? yes, and i will go home later.
say my request simply.
write a short conversation that asks about the stop and then asks why the person went there.
did the made up conversation give a name for the village?
no. it only said the village. a name was not needed to explain the difference.
what if i need to meet them?
then you need more detail, such as the specific station and a time. a general village area may not be enough for a real meeting.
what is the difference between i will read outside if it is quiet and i will read outside only if it is quiet?
if it is quiet gives one reason the outside reading will happen. only if it is quiet makes quiet a needed part of that choice: without quiet, the person will not read outside.
can you make that simple without saying i must read if it is quiet in both sentences?
with only if, quiet must be there before outside reading can happen. with if, the sentence says that quiet will lead to reading outside in this plan.
give an example for only if.
i will read outside only if it is quiet. if music is playing there and i cannot read, i will stay inside.
does the sentence with only if tell us i am outside already?
no. it gives a rule for the choice. it does not say what the place is like now or where the person is at this moment.
what if i say i am reading outside now and i kept that rule?
then you can use both details to say it is quiet enough under your rule. without knowing the rule was kept, being outside alone would not tell us that.
can you say the last part in simple words?
you said the rule was kept. with that detail, we can say the place had the quiet you needed before reading outside.
answer simply.
if the rule was kept, the quiet was there before you read outside.
tell me a story where a visit is over but the letter about it is not finished. keep those two things different.

a woman comes home after visiting her cousin. they spent the week cooking, walking, and talking near the garden. she wants to send a thank you letter, so she sits at her desk and writes the first line. then she stops to think about what part of the visit she wants to write about. her brother asks if the visit is still happening because the letter is not finished. she says no. the time with her cousin is over, but writing about it is something she is doing now.
say the part about taking time to think simply.
she stops to think about which part of the visit she wants to write about.
why are the visit and letter not the same task?
one is the time she spent with her cousin. the other is writing about that time after coming home. finishing one does not finish the other too.
answer simply.
the visit happened before the writing. she can finish the visit and still have a letter left to write.
write a short first line for her letter using only the story facts.
thank you for the week we spent cooking, walking, and talking together.
does that line need to say what happened on every day?
no. a short thank you can name things she enjoyed without giving every detail of the whole week.
answer simply.
no. the letter can say a few useful things without giving every detail.
i wrote the animal moved away. would changing animal to a more specific word tell you why it moved?
not by itself. a more specific word may give more detail about the animal, but the reason for moving still needs information from what happened.
answer simply.
no. a more specific word for the animal does not always tell us why it moved away.
what could i add to give the reason in a made up story?
you could say: the animal moved away because it heard a sound near the door. that gives a reason in your story.
say in the story in a short answer.
that gives a reason in your story.
does heard a sound tell us who made it?
no. it gives a sound as part of the reason, but not the person or thing making the sound. you would need another detail for that.
now make the sound come from someone putting a cup down near the door.
the animal moved away when someone put a cup down near the door and made a sound.
did the person mean to make the animal move?
the story does not say. a person can make a sound while doing something else without choosing what the animal will do.
answer with what the person wanted instead.
we do not know what the person wanted. the story only says that a sound happened and the animal moved away.
picoboi, if i say you know what i mean but i have not explained it, should you just choose an answer?
i should use the context you have given and ask if an important detail is not there. saying you know does not give me information you have not put into the conversation.
say that simply.
i can use what you told me. if a detail is not there, i should ask rather than make it up.
for example, i say bring the thing tomorrow, but i have talked about a book and a cup.
then i should ask which thing you mean: the book or the cup?
why not choose the book because it was said first?
being first does not tell us that it is the thing you want now. you talked about two objects, and i need to know which one your new request is about.
answer simply.
you talked about two things. i need to know which one is part of your request now.
i mean the cup. write the message clearly.
please bring the cup tomorrow.
does your question make the conversation less useful?
no. one useful question can help me give the right message instead of a clear message about the wrong thing.
